# Service

`customer_support.offering.service` · offering_family · parent `—`

> Work performed for one client at a time. The support consequence of "one at a time" is that demand is a series of individuals rather than a population: two clients reporting what sounds like the same complaint are usually reporting two genuinely different failures, because the engagements differ, the people differ and the deliverables differ. The fortieth ticket therefore carries as much new information as the first, which is the exact inverse of the product family and the reason nearly every product-support instinct misfires here. A fix is labour, not an asset. Retiring a class of future contact is largely impossible — there is no code change that helps the next client — so effort spent resolving does not compound, and the marginal cost of the forty-first resolution is the same as the first. That makes cost-to-serve a margin question rather than an efficiency question: a defect in a product costs a deploy, and a defect in a service costs the work being done twice by people who are billing. The second structural fact is that the boundary between support and delivery is contested and moves under commercial pressure. "Is this a bug or is it a change request?" has no technical answer; it is a scope conversation with a price attached, and it is the single most common source of dispute in this family. Support is frequently the function that discovers scope creep, and almost never the function permitted to price it. The habit an operator carries in from products and gets punished for is reflexive deflection. Writing an article, building a macro or pushing a client toward self-service reads as efficiency in a product queue and as neglect here — the client is paying for judgement applied to their situation, and a link to documentation is a refusal to supply it.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| delivery | people doing work for one client at a time; value sits in the engagement rather than in an artefact, and stops the moment the work stops |
| pricing_shape | time and materials, retainer, or fixed-fee against milestones — priced per hour or per outcome, never per copy |
| margin_profile | gross margin bounded by utilisation, so every hour of unbilled support is margin taken directly off the engagement it belongs to |
| post_sale_load | essentially all of the revenue depends on work done after signature; there is no point at which the deliverable is finished and safe |
| support_load | uncorrelated across clients and concentrated in a handful of engagements — usually the ones that were mis-scoped at sale. Volume tracks the number of live engagements and their health, not the number of users |
| resolution_locus | a human redoing or extending work. Occasionally the fix is in an artefact we built for this client alone, which is still not reusable — it helps exactly one account and the next client's version of the same problem starts from zero |
| notes | The commercially useful test for whether something is a service in the support sense is not how it is priced but whether the fix is reusable. Software sold on a retainer is still a product to support if one code change helps the next client; bespoke work billed as a subscription is still a service.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement`

Requires `plan`, `coverage_hours`, `expires_at`


> Entitlement in a service business is the statement of work, and it is the object that answers the family's defining question — is this covered, or is it a change request? A support organisation that cannot read the SOW at ticket time will do unbilled delivery and discover it at the end of the quarter, which is the characteristic financial failure of this family.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.commitment`

Requires `promised_at`, `due_at`, `owner_ref`


> Promises made in a service relationship are made by named people to named people and are remembered as personal undertakings rather than as contractual clocks. This is the object the client will quote back, and it outranks the SLA in every conversation that goes badly.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `requester_ref`, `customer_account_ref`


> Aggregation across the install base — the product family's central move — buys almost nothing here, because two clients' versions of the same complaint are usually different failures. What must be resolvable instead is the engagement: which account, which contract, which people. A service ticket without account context is unanswerable.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.churn_risk`

Requires `renewal_at`


> Service revenue is renewed as a whole engagement rather than lost a seat at a time, so churn is lumpy, binary and visible in the relationship long before it appears in usage data. The renewal date is the horizon every other signal has to be read against.

## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional**


> The two deactivations above are the most arguable claims in this file and should be argued with. They are correct for genuinely bespoke work and become wrong the moment a services firm productises — the same firm can have one engagement where deflection is an insult and another running on a shared platform where it is essential. That is what the managed_services type below exists to express, and it is why the deactivation sits at the family and is reversed at the type rather than being hedged in both places.
